messages.subject: DSM Diagnostics + Auto correlation
parts:
Hi All,

 

Apologies for asking another question so soon. After having read some of the responses on this group, I have tried to gear my questions so that they address what I have not yet seen. This question may be quite long-winded, so please bear with me: I have summarised the three main questions at the bottom.

 

I am modelling DSM over a grid cell of 500mx500m. My segment length is currently at 5km (which is at least twice the truncation distance of the detection function, and also not so long that it affects my spatial distribution with depth as a possible covariate). I aim to produce separate density surface models for cetaceans over two areas (A1 and A2) for three years of study. I am using the tweedie response variable due to overdispersion of zero data. I am using a detection function which has been obtained from pooling three years of study together, to fit a DSM for each year separately. I have read parts of Wood’s second edition introduction to GAM, which, although my brain hurts a little, has been very useful.

 

I am mostly interested in spatial distribution within a study area, and am not extrapolating outside the area, so a smooth of location (s(x,y)) is a good term to start with. I have also tried adding Depth to models as a smooth term to see if this improves.  From what I gather, if a significance of smooth p-value tends to 1, this should be removed from the model. What if none of the smooth terms show significance (i.e. p value >0.05 - for example in my summary(mod.24, p-value for s(x,y) = 0.594; however, this model shows highest deviance explained) should this be removed? I have also experimented with replacing bivariate smooth of location with two one dimensional smooths (s(x)+s(y)). In some instances, AIC favours individual smooths of location, but deviance explained for this model are usually smaller and none of the significance of smooths are below 0.05: e.g.

 

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
       edf Ref.df     F p-value
s(x) 1.715  2.128 0.499   0.687
s(y) 2.827  3.556 1.354   0.240

 

I remember reading somewhere that when using REML, using AIC for model selection is not advisable. Therefore, what is a preferred way of model guidance? Deviance explained or REML score?

 

I have attached the diagnostics of the “best” models guided from deviance explained for both A1 and A2, as well as a summary table for models describing A1. The table is to show example of how model selection would differ If I choose model using Deviance Explained compared to REML or AIC. 


Area A1
> summary(mod2)
 
Family: Tweedie(p=1.185) 
Link function: log 
 
Formula:
count ~ s(x, y, k = 30) + s(DEPTH, k = 7) + offset(off.set)
 
Parametric coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  -19.289      1.841  -10.48   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
 
Approximate significance of smooth terms:
           edf Ref.df     F p-value  
s(x,y)   8.462 11.123 1.965  0.0341 *
s(DEPTH) 1.797  2.124 1.353  0.2592  
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
 
R-sq.(adj) =  -0.098   Deviance explained = 49.1%
-REML = 125.87  Scale est. = 3.1175    n = 173
 
 
Area A2
> summary(mod24)
 
Family: Tweedie(p=1.292) 
Link function: log 
 
Formula:
count ~ s(x, y, k = 34) + DEPTH + offset(off.set)
 
Parametric coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -15.0664     0.3103 -48.553   <2e-16 ***
DEPTH        -0.1501     0.3206  -0.468    0.643    
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
 
Approximate significance of smooth terms:
         edf Ref.df     F p-value
s(x,y) 5.761  7.947 0.881   0.542
 
R-sq.(adj) =  -0.0588   Deviance explained = 22.9%
-REML = 76.323  Scale est. = 3.3402    n = 43


Gam.check for my study area A2 seems to fit better than A1. Area A1 shows high number of zero’s, but this may be due to the fact there are more segments in Area A1 and A1 was much larger in area than A2. Should I think of using different segment lengths for A1 (perhaps longer segments?).

 

Lastly, I am struggling to interpret correlation graphs. In my model for Area A1, there seems to be a spike at 1, 2 and so on, which from what I have found on the web means the spike has a value that is significantly different from zero. This means that the deviance is non-random? With a spike at 1 and 2, this means that my DSM is correlated with segments? I am confused and have difficulty in interpreting what this means (sorry my stats is a little rusty).



 

In summary:

  •         Does a significance of smooth p-value need to show significance (p<0.05) for it to be included in a model? What happens if none show significance..
  •         With REML method, is it not advisable to use AIC as model selection criteria, if so what Deviance explained a good candidate?
  •       What does the spike at a lag phase of 1 mean? That the segments are related/correlated to each other? Confused about the lagphase…

 

The more time I spend and the more I read other examples in this thread the more I feel confident with Distance, but I apologise if some of these questions here are rather basic. I would love to understand interpreting diagnostics a little better, so that I can use it in confidence with other studies further down the line. If there are any other recommendations for reading, other than Wood’s second edition of GAMs in R (which I am slowly reading my way through) I would greatly appreciate it. 

Thanks

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM Diagnostics + Auto correlation
parts:
Hi Raph, hi listfolk,

Quick reply to your three questions:

- On p-values: bear in mind the test p-value is for. It's asking
(roughly), "is this smooth different from a line at 0". Graphically: can
you draw a straight line through the confidence band around the smooth.
A non-significant p-value might be because the term is unrelated to the
counts you saw or just because there is a lot of uncertainty around that
smooth. If a smooth of space is not significant and you don't have other
terms in the model, that might be an indication that your data don't
require a spatial model (since their distribution doesn't seem to vary
in space).

- If REML is used you cannot compare REML scores. BUT you can compare AIC.

- Spike at lag 1 in the correlogram means that segments that are direct
neighbours (either side) are correlated. I'm less of a fan of these
diagnostics as I think they're often a bit hard to interpret, you might
find the practical solutions from the recent spatial modelling course
here useful: http://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-dsm-2020/ in
particular the part on model checking may help.


Hope this is useful!

cheers,
--dave

Raph
